newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK-Housing, Beige Book, 2-yr notes.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK-Housing, Beige Book, 2-yr notes.

text.p: A report on the U.S. housing market, an anecdotal account of the nation's business conditions, and a two-year Treasury note auction will be the landmarks of Wednesday's U.S. government securities trading session, market participants said.
The December U.S. housing starts report, due at 0830 EST/1330 GMT, is expected to show that starts slipped in the last month of the year after surging in November.
December housing starts occurred at an annualized rate of 1.47 million in December, economists said in a Reuters poll.
That rate represents a decline from an annualized 1.514 million starts recorded in November.

"Housing starts should be down a little from last month," said Lee Youngdahl, economist at Aubrey G. Lanston & Co. "There are no great shakes there. We had a big pop (up) in November. We'll probably unwind a little of that in December, but it's still a healthy level of housing activity."
If housing starts fall more sharply than the market expects, "that would be seen as a reason to extend Tuesday's rally," said Chris Rupkey, vice president and economist at Bank of Tokyo/Mitsubishi.
Bond prices rallied on Tuesday after testimony by Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan struck the bond market as straightforward and not alarming.
The 6-3/4 percent 30-year bond finished at 96-11/32, up 17/32 to yield 6.79 percent.

At 1400 EST/1800 GMT, the Federal Reserve will release its Beige Book, a periodic account of business conditions around the nation based largely on anecdotal observations gathered in the various regions of the Federal Reserve system.
"Traditionally, the market doesn't respond much to the Beige Book," said Rupkey.

"The Beige Book shouldn't pose any great surprise," said Youngdahl. "There still will be claims that growth remains moderate, that wage pressures are roughly in check. The Beige Book is kind of a non-event in the scheme of things."
The biggest suspense for the session is focused on how much demand the market will generate for the $17.5 billion in two-year notes the Treasury will auction on Wednesday.

"The two-year note will be important," said Rupkey, "The pricing will tell us a lot about what people expect for Fed policy in the next two or three months -- certainly through the March 25 FOMC (Federal Open Market Committee) meeting."
The two-year notes scheduled for sale on Wednesday ended with a 5.99 percent yield on a when-issued basis on Tuesday, 74 basis points above the 5-1/4 percent Federal funds rate.
"If people were really concerned about a tightening in the next two or three months, this spread would be about 100 basis points," Rupkey said.
With a closing bond yield of 6.79 percent on Tuesday, a challenge of the 6.75 percent level may be near, Rupkey said.
"If we get through that level, it will cause more people to...bet that the next direction is up," he said.
Youngdahl was more dubious.

"In terms of the two-year note, six percent to me does not represent significant value considering the fact that the Fed might be engineering one or two (interest rate) tightenings before spring is out," said Youngdahl.
Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities America Inc, said that with Greenspan's testimony ended and bonds left unrattled by it, the two-year note sale could go very well.
"The increase in prices we saw on Tuesday suggests a bit of an upbeat mood in the market," said Moran. "I think it will be a good auction at current levels."
Dealers indicated that Federal funds would open between 5-1/4 percent and 5-5/16 percent on Wednesday.
